title: A Family With More Than One Shape
subtitle: Love & Duty · Chapter 26 of 40
content:
Hakoda asked Aang to go fishing.

Aang looked at the bucket of bait.

Then at Hakoda.

Then at the bucket again.

“I’m vegetarian.”

Hakoda nodded. “The fish aren’t.”

Toph laughed for an entire minute.

The trip was not actually about fish.

Everyone knew this except Aang, who spent the first half hour trying to design a morally acceptable system in which he could help catch dinner without personally participating in the catching of dinner.

“You can steer,” Hakoda finally said.

Aang brightened.

“I can steer.”

Katara watched them leave from the dock.

“He’s going to interrogate him.”

Sokka, beside her, shook his head. “Dad doesn’t interrogate.”

“He absolutely interrogates.”

“He has conversations with tactical objectives.”

“That is an interrogation.”

Toph leaned toward me. “Water Tribe people are weird.”

“You’re dating two of them.”

“A continuing error.”

Katara shoved her shoulder.

Hakoda’s tactical conversation was only the beginning.

By the second day in the South, it became clear that our relationship was going to be discussed whether we wanted it to be or not—not with hostility, exactly, but with the enthusiastic curiosity of a community where privacy had historically been limited by population size and weather.

An aunt asked Katara how sleeping arrangements worked.

Katara nearly inhaled her tea.

A cousin asked Toph whether she and Katara were “actually together or just spiritually adjacent.”

Toph answered, “Depends who’s asking and how much money they have.”

A grandmother I had never met patted my hand and told me I looked too thin for three partners.

I did not know what that meant.

Sokka refused to help.

“This is incredible,” he said.

“You’re enjoying my suffering.”

“It’s the only affordable entertainment down here.”

The real conversation happened after dinner on the third night.

Gran Gran sat by the fire mending a glove. Hakoda carved a new handle for a kitchen knife. Sokka was inventing something on the floor that involved springs and made Katara nervous.

Aang had gone outside with Appa.

Toph was lying across two cushions with her head in Katara’s lap.

Gran Gran looked at the three of us.

“So.”

Every muscle in my body tightened.

Toph whispered, “Run.”

Katara pinched her ear.

Gran Gran continued stitching.

“When your grandfather and I married, everyone in my village had an opinion.”

Katara’s face softened.

“When your mother married Hakoda, everyone had an opinion.”

Hakoda looked up. “Most of them were wrong.”

“Some were correct,” Gran Gran said.

Hakoda wisely returned to the knife handle.

Gran Gran tied off the thread.

“People like to believe the shape of a family tells them whether the people inside are good.”

Toph stopped pretending to sleep.

Gran Gran’s gaze moved from Katara to me.

“It doesn’t.”

The room quieted.

“A marriage can be cruel. A household can be kind. Blood can protect you. Blood can fail you. Tradition can hold people together and it can hold them still.”

Katara swallowed.

This was not abstract in their family.

Gran Gran had left the Northern Water Tribe because its customs would have dictated her marriage and life. Katara had challenged the North’s refusal to teach women combat. Toph had run from a wealthy home because love there had become a cage.

Aang carried the memory of a culture nearly destroyed.

We all had reasons to distrust anyone who treated one family structure as proof of morality.

Gran Gran looked at Toph.

“Do they let you leave?”

Toph sat up.

The question surprised all of us.

“Yes.”

“Do they listen when you say no?”

“Yes.”

“Do they make decisions about your body?”

“No.”

Gran Gran nodded.

Then she looked at Katara.

“Can you be angry without them being afraid of you?”

Katara’s eyes filled before she could stop them.

“Yes.”

Gran Gran looked at me.

“Can you be useless sometimes?”

I laughed because the alternative was crying.

“I’m practicing.”

“Practice harder.”

Toph pointed at Gran Gran. “I really like her.”

Finally Gran Gran looked toward the door Aang had gone through.

“And can he be a man in your home instead of the Avatar every minute?”

Nobody answered immediately.

That question belonged to all of us.

Katara said, “We try.”

Gran Gran returned to her glove.

“Then you are doing what every family does. Trying to build something people can live inside.”

Sokka lifted his head from the spring mechanism.

“Can I quote you when people ask me about them?”

“No.”

“Worth a shot.”

Later I found Aang outside beside Appa, brushing snow from the bison’s fur.

“How was fishing?”

“We caught nothing.”

“Successful vegetarian fishing.”

“Exactly.”

He smiled, then looked toward the house.

“Hakoda asked if I’m serious about all of you.”

I leaned against the fence.

“What did you say?”

“That I don’t know what forever means at twenty-one.”

The honesty surprised me.

Aang continued brushing Appa.

“But I know I don’t want any of you treated like temporary parts of my life just because other people understand Katara and me more easily.”

Something warm moved through my chest.

“He liked that answer?”

“He said it was better than pretending.”

“Gran Gran would approve.”

Aang looked at me.

“What did she say?”

I told him.

When I reached the question about whether he could be a man instead of the Avatar, Aang went quiet.

Appa rumbled softly.

“I don’t know how to turn it off,” he said.

“Maybe you don’t.”

He looked down.

“Maybe the question is whether you’re allowed to put it down sometimes, even if it’s still there.”

Aang leaned the brush against the fence.

“What am I when I put it down?”

There was no self-pity in the question.

That made it sadder.

He had been the Avatar since twelve in every public story about him. Even before that, he had been a prodigy. A monk. A survivor he had not chosen to become.

I stepped closer.

“You’re the person who puts his cold feet on me in bed.”

Aang blinked.

“You sing to Appa when you think nobody can hear.”

Appa huffed.

“You cheat at tile games by pretending you misunderstood the rules.”

“I do not.”

“You absolutely do.”

“I adapt.”

“You steal fruit from Katara’s plate even though she will always catch you.”

His mouth twitched.

“You apologize to furniture when you bump into it.”

“That happened once.”

“Three times.”

Aang laughed.

I reached for his hand.

“You’re Aang.”

His fingers closed around mine.

“Is that enough?”

“For me.”

The answer came easily.

That night, the family gathered around one long table.

Not our four-bowl table.

A bigger one.

Hakoda. Gran Gran. Sokka. Cousins. Neighbors who might as well have been relatives. Children asleep against adult shoulders. Toph arguing over cards with an uncle who did not care that she could detect lies because he cheated with such confidence it became art.

Katara moved through all of it differently than she moved at home.

Not more herself.

Another self.

Daughter. Sister. Southern Water Tribe. The girl who had once stared toward the horizon waiting for a father at war.

Aang sat beside her, not demanding the version of Katara that belonged to him.

Toph sat on her other side, learning the rhythm of a family through floorboards and voices.

I sat across from them and understood something Gran Gran had not said aloud.

A family with more than one shape did not need to flatten itself into one role.

Katara could be daughter here and lover later.

Aang could be Avatar in the morning and a terrible card player at night.

Toph could be independent and still lean against my shoulder when she was tired.

I could belong without pretending I had always been here.

After dinner, Gran Gran handed me a repaired mitten.

“This isn’t mine.”

“It is now.”

I looked at the careful stitching.

No ceremony.

No declaration.

A practical object made to keep me warm.

I put it on.

It fit badly.

I loved it.

Hakoda did not ask me what my intentions were.

I had prepared three answers anyway.

Instead, while repairing a net beside the fire, he said, “Katara trusts you.”

Every prepared sentence vanished.

“I hope so.”

“She does.”

He pulled a knot tight. “Toph too, though I’m not sure she trusts anyone in a way that looks normal.”

“That sounds accurate.”

“And Aang.”

At his name, Hakoda smiled with an expression I could not quite read. Affection, worry, the complicated awareness of watching someone who had once been a child become responsible for too much.

“I’m not asking you to take care of them,” he said.

Relief came so fast it embarrassed me.

“Good.”

His laugh was quiet. “You’ve heard that before?”

“In several forms.”

“People like assigning jobs when they don’t understand a family.”

He handed me part of the net. “Hold that.”

I did.

“My job,” he continued, “is not to decide what shape makes Katara happy.”

Across the camp, Katara was arguing with Sokka about whether he had deliberately taught Aang the wrong fishing technique. Aang defended himself with increasing desperation. Toph sat on a crate giving unhelpful commentary.

Hakoda followed my attention.

“My job is to notice whether she gets to be herself inside it.”

I looked back at him.

“That seems fair.”

“It is also what I expect her to notice for you.”

The net tightened between our hands.

Family with more than one shape did not mean nobody outside it had questions.

Sometimes the good questions were the ones that did not demand a particular answer.
